blocks.text:
Before Java 8, passing behaviour to a method meant writing an anonymous class: five lines of ceremony to say "compare by length". Lambda expressions (Java 8, 2014) give you a short syntax for exactly that case: a piece of code you hand to another method to run later. The whole Stream API, `CompletableFuture`, `Optional.map`, `Comparator.comparing` and most of modern Spring code are built on this one idea. If you understand lambdas well enough to predict what they capture, what `this` means inside them and how they compile, the rest of this Part becomes easy.

### Functional interfaces: the type of a lambda

A lambda has no type of its own. It is always converted to an instance of a **functional interface**: an interface with exactly one abstract method (default, static and private methods do not count, and neither do abstract methods that merely re-declare `Object` methods such as `equals`). The compiler decides which interface from the context. This is called **target typing**: the type the surrounding code expects is the type of the lambda.

blocks.code:
interface Validator<T> { boolean test(T t); }

Validator<String> notBlank = s -> !s.isBlank();     // target type: Validator<String>
Function<Integer, Integer> inc  = x -> x + 1;      // same text, different target type
UnaryOperator<Integer>     inc2 = x -> x + 1;      // ... also fine
blocks.title: Lam1.java (excerpt)

blocks.text: The lambda `x -> x + 1` is not "a function"; it is whatever the left-hand side says it is. The parameter types are inferred from the target type, so you normally write `s -> ...` and not `(String s) -> ...`. You may write the types, or use `var`, but you must not mix styles in one parameter list.

An expression body returns its value (or nothing, for a `void` target). A block body behaves like a method body. A lambda whose body is a single method call such as `s -> System.out.println(s)` is compatible with both value-returning and `void` targets; the compiler picks whichever fits.

### The java.util.function toolbox

You rarely need to declare your own functional interface, because `java.util.function` has 43 of them. They look intimidating but follow a naming scheme. Learn the five core shapes and the rest are variations.

rows: Function where all types are the same
blocks.caption: The five core functional interfaces.

blocks.text: The variations are mechanical: a `Bi` prefix means two arguments (`BiFunction<T,U,R>`, `BiConsumer`, `BiPredicate`); `Int`, `Long`, `Double` prefixes are primitive specialisations that avoid boxing (`IntPredicate`, `ToIntFunction<T>`, `IntBinaryOperator`, `IntSupplier`). `Runnable` and `Callable<V>` are the older no-argument shapes from `java.lang` and `java.util.concurrent`.

$ java Lam1.java
true false
2 2
Effective Java
Java Puzzlers
Book: Tiny Book
5 20
true
12 11
105
2
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `inc.andThen(dbl)` runs `inc` first then `dbl`: (5+1) times 2 = 12. `inc.compose(dbl)` runs `dbl` first: 5 times 2 plus 1 =

1. Mixing these two up is a classic mistake.

- `Predicate` gives you `and`, `or`, `negate` as default methods; `Function` gives `andThen`, `compose`, `identity()`. Small combinators like these are how you build behaviour from parts.
- `Book::new` works as a `BiFunction<String,Integer,Book>` because the record's canonical constructor takes `(String, int)`; the compiler matches shapes, boxing as needed.

### Declaring your own: @FunctionalInterface

When none of the standard shapes carries meaning, declare your own, and annotate it with `@FunctionalInterface`. The annotation changes nothing at run time; it tells the compiler "fail the build if someone adds a second abstract method", which would silently break every lambda that targets the interface. Use it for any interface you intend lambdas to implement.

blocks.title: Retry.java

blocks.text:
A custom interface is also the standard answer to a limit of the built-in ones: `Function.apply` cannot throw checked exceptions, but your own `attempt()` can. Section "Functional style in practice" in the last chapter of this Part returns to this.

### Capturing variables: effectively final

A lambda body may use local variables from the enclosing method, but only if they are **effectively final**: never reassigned after initialisation (you do not need to write `final`). The lambda captures the variable's *value*, copies it, and carries the copy with it, possibly to another thread, long after the method returned.

blocks.title: Capture.java (fragment)

blocks.text:
Why the rule? A local variable lives in a stack frame that disappears when the method returns, and may be read by a different thread. Allowing the lambda to write a stack variable would make "shared mutable local" a thing, with all the races that implies. Instance fields and static fields are different: they live on the heap and a lambda can read and write them freely (and then you own the thread-safety problem).

The common workarounds, in order of preference: do not mutate at all (use `mapToInt(...).sum()` or a collector, which is the point of the next chapters); use an `AtomicInteger` or `LongAdder` when several threads are involved; or, for single-threaded throwaway code, a one-element array as in the listing above (`counter[0]++`). The array reference is final; its contents are not. This works but is a smell: if you need it often, you are probably writing a loop in disguise.

### What does this mean inside a lambda?

In an anonymous class, `this` refers to the anonymous object itself. In a lambda, `this` refers to the **enclosing** **instance**: a lambda is not a new scope for `this`, it is just code that lives in the enclosing method. A lambda also cannot declare a local variable with the same name as one in the enclosing scope (an anonymous class can shadow it).

blocks.title: Lam2.java

blocks.code:
$ java Lam2.java
lambda this = outer Lam2
anon this = Lam2$1
X hello bob 4 [] 3
true true
false
Runnable
true
false
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- Inside the lambda, `this.name` compiled and `getClass()` reported `Lam2`: `this` is the enclosing `Lam2`. In the anonymous class it is a different object of class `Lam2$1`.
- The last two lines show a detail that is **not** a guarantee: a lambda that captures nothing may be a single cached instance (`sup() == sup()` was `true` here), while a capturing one is a fresh object per evaluation. Never depend on identity of lambdas. The Language Specification explicitly leaves it open.

### Method references: four kinds

When a lambda does nothing but call one existing method, a **method reference** says it more briefly. There are four kinds and the one everybody gets wrong is the third.

blocks.caption: The four kinds of method reference.

blocks.text: In the unbound form the *first* parameter of the functional interface becomes the receiver: `Function<String,Integer>` `f = String::length` means `s -> s.length()`. That is also why `Comparator.comparing(Book::title)` works. A bound reference such as `System.out::println` evaluates `System.out` once, when the reference is created; the lambda `x ->` `System.out.println(x)` would read the field every time. Prefer a method reference when it is shorter *and* clearer; if you have to think about which kind it is, write the lambda.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: A method reference is ambiguous if the method is overloaded in a way that fits several shapes. `Integer::toString` fails as a `Function<Integer,String>` because both the static `Integer.toString(int)` and the instance `toString()` fit. Use a lambda, `i -> i.toString()`, or `String::valueOf`.

### How lambdas compile: invokedynamic, not inner classes

A natural guess is that the compiler turns each lambda into an anonymous inner class. It does not, and the difference matters for startup time, memory and even stack traces. Compile this tiny program and look at the bytecode.

$ javap -c -p -cp out Lam3

    Code:
       0: invokedynamic #7,  0     // InvokeDynamic #0:apply:()LLam3$Op;

       6: aload_1

      13: aload_2
      14: invokeinterface #15,  1  // InterfaceMethod java/lang/Runnable.run:()V
      19: return

  private static void lambda$main$1(Lam3$Op);
    Code:
       ...
       6: invokeinterface #25,  3  // InterfaceMethod Lam3$Op.apply:(II)I

  private static int lambda$main$0(int, int);
    Code:

blocks.text:
How it works at run time:

1. The first time the JVM executes an `invokedynamic` instruction, it calls its **bootstrap method**, listed in the class file's `BootstrapMethods` attribute. For lambdas this is `LambdaMetafactory.metafactory`.
2. The metafactory receives the target interface (`Op`), the method handle for the synthetic body (`REF_invokeStatic` `Lam3.lambda$main$0`) and the captured arguments' types. It spins up a small hidden class at run time that implements the interface and delegates to the body.
3. It returns a `CallSite`. The JVM permanently links that instruction to it, so later executions skip the bootstrap and, with no captured variables, can hand back one shared instance.

Why not inner classes? An anonymous class is fixed at compile time: one `.class` file per lambda to load, verify and keep in Metaspace, even if never run. With `invokedynamic` the compiler emits a *recipe* and the strategy is chosen by the runtime. The translation can improve across JDK releases without recompiling your code; this is the same trick used for string concatenation (`makeConcatWithConstants`, visible in the `javap` output above). The cost is some startup work on the first use of each lambda, which is one reason a Java program that uses many lambdas starts a little slower on a cold JVM and why AOT caching features target it.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Lambda classes are *hidden classes*: you cannot find them by name, they do not show up in `Class.forName`, and in a stack trace they appear as frames like `Lam2$$Lambda/0x000...run`, usually filtered out. The synthetic body method `lambda$main$0` does appear in stack traces; that is the frame you will read when a lambda throws.

### Pitfalls and good practice

- **Keep lambdas short.** More than three or four lines: extract a named method and use a method reference. A name documents intent and gives you a clean stack frame.
- **Do not capture what you do not need.** A lambda that uses an instance field or method captures `this`. If you store it in a long-lived registry (a listener list, a cache), you keep the whole enclosing object alive: the same leak pattern as an inner class.
- **Checked exceptions** cannot cross a standard functional interface. Wrap in an unchecked exception or use your own interface (see `Retry` above).
- **Avoid overloads that differ only in functional interface type** (`submit(Runnable)` vs `submit(Callable)`): lambdas are often ambiguous between them. `ExecutorService.submit` gets away with it only because a lambda with a return value cannot be a `Runnable`.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How are lambdas different from anonymous inner classes? (1) `this` refers to the enclosing instance, not the lambda. (2) A lambda is compiled to a private synthetic method plus an `invokedynamic` call site bootstrapped by `LambdaMetafactory`; an anonymous class is a separate `.class` file loaded at class-load time. (3) A lambda can only implement a functional interface (one abstract method); an anonymous class can extend a class or implement any interface and can hold state. (4) A lambda's identity is unspecified (it may be cached); an anonymous class creates a new object each time.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why must captured local variables be effectively final? The lambda gets a copy of the value, and it may run later or on another thread after the frame is gone. If the variable could change, the copy and the original would silently disagree, or threads would race on a stack slot. The rule turns the problem into a compile-time error. Fields are not restricted because they live on the heap, not in the frame.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A lambda is an instance of a functional interface, whose type comes from the context (target typing).

- Memorise the five core shapes: `Function`, `Predicate`, `Consumer`, `Supplier`, and the operator variants; the rest are `Bi`/primitive variations.
- Captured locals must be effectively final; `this` in a lambda is the enclosing instance.
- There are four method reference kinds; the unbound one (`String::length`) takes the receiver as the first argument.
- Lambdas compile to a private synthetic method plus `invokedynamic` and `LambdaMetafactory`, not to inner class files.

Tony Hoare called the null reference his "billion dollar mistake". A method that returns `Member` might return a member or `null`, and nothing in the signature tells the caller. The caller who forgets the check gets a `NullPointerException` far from the cause. `java.util.Optional<T>` (Java 8) is a small container that is either empty or holds one non-null value, so the *return type itself* says "this may be absent" and forces the caller to deal with it.

### Design intent: a return type, not a field type

The Javadoc is explicit: `Optional` is intended for use as a **method return type** where there is a clear need to represent "no result" and `null` would likely cause errors. It is not meant as a replacement for every nullable reference. In particular, do not use it for fields, method parameters, collection elements or map values. It is not `Serializable`, it adds an object allocation, and a parameter of type `Optional<String>` can itself be `null`, which defeats the purpose.

### Creating and consuming

There are exactly three ways to create one: `Optional.of(x)` (x must be non-null, otherwise NPE immediately), `Optional.ofNullable(x)` (empty if x is null) and `Optional.empty()`. Everything else is a way of getting something *out*, or transforming it without leaving the box.

#### What to notice

- **Transform, do not unwrap.** `find(id).map(Member::email).filter(...).orElse(...)` is a chain with no `if` and no `null`. Member 2 has an email of `null`; `map` turns a `null` result into an empty `Optional`, so the chain keeps working. Member 3 does not exist at all and takes the same path.
- `orElse` **evaluates its argument eagerly.** "(computing default)" printed even though the member had an email. `orElseGet(supplier)` only calls the supplier when the `Optional` is empty. Use `orElse` for cheap constants and `orElseGet` for anything that does work (a database call, object construction, logging).
- `map` **vs** `flatMap`**.** `map(f)` wraps whatever `f` returns, so a function that already returns an `Optional` produces `Optional<Optional<String>>`. Use `flatMap` when your function returns an `Optional`: it flattens one level. This is the same relationship you will see between `Stream.map` and `Stream.flatMap`.
- `Optional::stream` (Java 9) turns an `Optional` into a stream of zero or one element. `flatMap(Optional::stream)` is the idiomatic way to drop the empties from a stream of optionals.
- `orElseThrow()` with no arguments (Java 10) is the clear, intention-revealing replacement for `get()`. It throws `NoSuchElementException`, but its name says so.

blocks.text:
### Primitive optionals

`OptionalInt`, `OptionalLong` and `OptionalDouble` hold a primitive and avoid boxing. They are what `IntStream.max()`, `average()` and friends return. They have `getAsInt()`, `orElse`, `ifPresent`, `isPresent` but no `map`/`filter`, because they exist for the end of a primitive stream rather than for chaining. Note that `average()` of an empty stream is an empty `OptionalDouble`, not `NaN`; that is why the example printed `-1.0` using `orElse(-1)`.

### Anti-patterns

#### 1. isPresent() followed by get()

This is a null check wearing a costume, and it gains nothing:

blocks.title: Anti1.java (fragment)

blocks.text:
#### 2. Optional as a parameter, field or collection element

`void register(Optional<String> nickname)` forces every caller to wrap, can still be passed `null`, and communicates less than two overloads or a nullable parameter with documentation. A field of type `Optional` is not serialisable and doubles the object count. Return `Optional` from the *getter* of a possibly-absent field instead: `Optional<String>` `nickname() { return Optional.ofNullable(nickname); }`.

#### 3. Returning null from a method that returns Optional

The worst of both worlds: `return null;` where `Optional.empty()` was meant. Callers trust the type and call `.map` on a null reference.

#### 4. Using Optional for collections

Return an empty `List`, not `Optional<List<T>>`. An empty collection already means "nothing".

#### 5. Optional.get() without a check, and orElse(null)

`get()` in code review is a red flag: prefer `orElseThrow()` so the failure mode is stated. `orElse(null)` re-introduces the null you were avoiding; it is acceptable only at a boundary with an API that demands null.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: `Optional` is a value-based class. Do not use it as a lock for `synchronized`, do not compare with `==` (use `equals`) and do not rely on identity. Equality is defined by the contained values: `Optional.of("a").equals(Optional.of("a"))` is `true`.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In Spring Data, repository methods such as `CrudRepository.findById(id)` return `Optional<T>`, and `Optional` works well with `orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(id))` in services, which a controller advice then maps to HTTP 404. Spring MVC also supports `Optional<T>` for optional `@RequestParam` values, which is one of the few cases of `Optional` as a parameter that the framework itself handles for you.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between `orElse` and `orElseGet`, and between `map` and `flatMap` on `Optional`? `orElse(x)` evaluates `x` eagerly even if a value is present; `orElseGet(supplier)` invokes the supplier only if empty, so use it when the default is expensive or has side effects. `map(f)` wraps the result of `f` in an `Optional` (and turns a `null` result into empty); `flatMap(f)` expects `f` to return an `Optional` already and avoids the double wrapping.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
`Optional<T>` is a return type that makes "may be absent" explicit; do not use it for fields, parameters or collections.

- Create with `of`, `ofNullable`, `empty`; transform with `map`, `flatMap`, `filter`; leave with `orElse`, `orElseGet`, `orElseThrow`, `ifPresentOrElse`.
- `orElse` is eager, `orElseGet` is lazy; `flatMap` flattens an `Optional` returned by the function.
- `isPresent()` plus `get()` is a null check in disguise; chain instead. Never return `null` from an `Optional` method.
- `OptionalInt`, `OptionalLong`, `OptionalDouble` avoid boxing and end primitive-stream pipelines.

A loop tells the computer *how* to process data: create an accumulator, iterate, test, add. A stream pipeline states *what* you want: "the titles of the long books, upper-cased". Streams (Java 8, package `java.util.stream`) are a way to describe a computation over a sequence of elements as a pipeline of steps, and then let the library run it. They are not a data structure: a stream stores nothing, it is a view over a source that carries a recipe.

### Anatomy of a pipeline

Every pipeline has three parts:

1. A **source** that produces elements: a collection (`list.stream()`), an array (`Arrays.stream(a)`), a generator (`Stream.iterate`), a range (`IntStream.range`), a file (`Files.lines`), and so on.
2. Zero or more **intermediate operations** (`filter`, `map`, `sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`, `flatMap`, `peek` ...). Each returns a new stream. They are lazy: calling them does no work.
3. Exactly one **terminal operation** (`collect`, `toList`, `forEach`, `count`, `reduce`, `findFirst`, `anyMatch`, `sum` ...). It triggers the whole pipeline and produces a result or a side effect.

#### What to notice

- "pipeline built, nothing printed yet": creating the pipeline ran no `peek`. Work started only at `toList()`.
- The order is `peek1 kiwi, peek2 kiwi, peek1 apple, peek2 apple`: each element travels through the *entire* chain before the next one starts. It is not "filter everything, then map everything".
- After `limit(2)` was satisfied, the source stopped being consumed: `fig`, `banana`, `cherry` and `date` never appeared. This is **short-circuiting**.
- The elements that were filtered out never reach `peek2` (in this run only `kiwi` and `apple` got that far, because `limit(2)` ended the traversal).
- Reusing a stream throws `IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed`. A stream is **one-shot**. If you need to traverse twice, create a new stream from the source, or keep a `Supplier<Stream<T>>`.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Prefer the primitive streams `IntStream`, `LongStream` and `DoubleStream` for numbers. They avoid boxing and have `sum()`, `average()`, `max()` and `summaryStatistics()`. Convert with `mapToInt`, `mapToObj`, `boxed()`, `asLongStream()`.

### Intermediate operations

The ones you use daily: `filter(Predicate)` keeps matching elements; `map(Function)` transforms each element; `flatMap(Function<T, Stream<R>>)` maps each element to a stream and concatenates them; `distinct()`, `sorted()`, `limit(n)`, `skip(n)`, `peek`, `takeWhile`, `dropWhile`, `mapMulti`.

`flatMap` is where people stall. `map` is one-to-one; `flatMap` is one-to-many (or one-to-none): each element becomes a stream, and the streams are joined into one. With `List<List<Integer>>`, `flatMap(List::stream)` gives a flat stream of integers, and an inner empty list simply contributes nothing. It is the stream counterpart of `Optional.flatMap` from the previous chapter.

`mapMulti` (Java 16) is the imperative cousin. Instead of returning a stream, your function receives each element plus a sink and may push zero, one or many outputs. It avoids allocating a small stream per element and is handy when the "expansion" is conditional. Because of type inference, you often have to give the output type explicitly (`<Integer>mapMulti`).

`takeWhile` **and** `dropWhile` (Java 9) work on the encounter order: `takeWhile` returns the longest prefix satisfying the predicate and stops; `dropWhile` discards that prefix and returns the rest. Unlike `filter`, they stop evaluating the predicate at the first failure, so on `1, 2, 3, 10, 1, 2` with `x < 5`, `takeWhile` gives `[1, 2, 3]` and `dropWhile` gives `[10, 1, 2]` (see the output above). Use them only on ordered streams.

### Terminal operations and short-circuiting

A **short-circuiting** operation can finish without consuming the whole stream: `findFirst`, `findAny`, `anyMatch`, `allMatch`, `noneMatch`, and the intermediate `limit`/`takeWhile`. This is what makes infinite streams usable: `Stream.iterate(1, x -> x * 2).limit(8)` is fine; `Stream.iterate(...).count()` never returns.

`reduce` folds elements into one value. `reduce(0, Integer::sum)` takes an *identity* and an associative function and returns the value itself; `reduce(Integer::max)` has no identity, so it returns an `Optional` (the stream might be empty). The three-argument form `reduce(identity, accumulator, combiner)` exists for parallel streams and for when the result type differs from the element type (see `Str2` below, where it sums lengths). For most real tasks a collector (next chapter) or a primitive `sum()` is clearer.

### Statefulness, ordering and what "behavioural parameters" must obey

Intermediate operations are either **stateless** (`filter`, `map`, `flatMap`, `peek`: each element is handled on its own) or **stateful** (`sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`, `skip`: need to remember or see other elements). `sorted` is a full barrier: it cannot emit anything until the upstream is exhausted. The second program shows that, and the other rules the Javadoc imposes on lambdas passed to stream operations.

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `findFirst` stopped as soon as the first element that matched (`b`) arrived: `visit c` and `visit d` never printed.
- With `sorted()`, all three "before sort" lines print before any "after sort" line, and `limit(1)` then needed only one element downstream. Every element had to be pulled upstream first. This is why `sorted()` on a huge or infinite stream is a trap.
- Vertical processing is visible in the third block: `p1 a, p2 A, p1 b, p2 B`.
- Modifying the source collection while the pipeline runs is **interference** and breaks the contract. For an `ArrayList` source the stream throws `ConcurrentModificationException` (the message is "CME" in our output, printed by the catch block). Do not rely on this detection; just do not do it.
- `forEach(sink::add)` into an `ArrayList` works sequentially but is a side effect on shared state; on a parallel stream it would corrupt the list. Use `collect` or `toList()`.

The rules for behavioural parameters (lambdas you pass in) are short and worth memorising:

- They should be **non-interfering**: do not modify the stream's source during the pipeline.
- They should be **stateless**: the result must not depend on anything that may change during execution, such as a counter or a `HashSet` you are filling. Otherwise results differ between sequential and parallel runs and between runs.
- Side effects are best confined to `forEach` at the end; `peek` is for debugging.

### Encounter order

A stream has an **encounter order** if its source does (a `List`, an array, `Stream.of`; not a `HashSet`). `sorted` imposes one; `unordered()` removes the requirement. Most operations preserve it. This matters in two places: `findFirst`, `limit` and `takeWhile` are defined in terms of order (so they are costlier on parallel streams), and `forEach` on a parallel stream does not respect it (`forEachOrdered` does, at a price).

### toList() versus collect(Collectors.toList())

`Stream.toList()` (Java 16) returns an **unmodifiable** list and permits `null` elements; the last line of the first program showed `UnsupportedOperationException` on `add`. `collect(Collectors.toList())` returns "a `List`" with no guarantees about mutability or type (in practice an `ArrayList`). Use `toList()` by default; use `collect(Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new))` when you really need a mutable list. Both are covered in the next chapter.

### Streams versus loops

Streams shine for filter-transform-collect pipelines, grouping and aggregation. A plain loop is better when you need to mutate local state, early-`return` from a method, handle checked exceptions, or when the pipeline would have more than five or six steps with nested lambdas. Streams are not faster: for small collections an equivalent loop is typically the same speed or quicker; the benefit is readability. The final chapter of this Part returns to this trade-off.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Do not use a stream when you only need `forEach`. `list.stream().forEach(...)` is just `list.forEach(...)` with extra steps. And never write `stream.map(x -> { sideEffect(x); return x; })` expecting it to run: with a terminal operation like `count()` the JVM may legitimately skip the whole pipeline when it can compute the answer directly from the source size (since Java 9 `list.stream().map(...).count()` does not run `map` on a sized source).

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between intermediate and terminal operations, and why are streams lazy? Intermediate operations return a new stream and only describe the work; the terminal operation triggers execution. Laziness lets the library fuse the stages into one pass with no intermediate collections, and short-circuit (`limit`, `findFirst`, `anyMatch`) so only as many elements are processed as needed. It also makes infinite streams usable.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Can you reuse a stream? What is the difference between `map` and `flatMap`? No: a stream can be consumed only once; a second terminal operation throws `IllegalStateException`. `map` transforms each element one-to-one; `flatMap` maps each element to a stream and flattens the results into one, so it is one-to-many.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A stream is a lazy, one-shot pipeline: source, intermediate operations, one terminal operation.

- Nothing runs until the terminal operation; elements flow through the chain one at a time and short-circuit operations stop early.
- `map` is one-to-one, `flatMap` is one-to-many, `mapMulti` is the push-style alternative; `takeWhile`/`dropWhile` act on prefixes.
- Stateful operations (`sorted`, `distinct`) are barriers; lambdas must be non-interfering and stateless.
- Prefer `toList()`, primitive streams and collectors over manual mutation; use a loop when a loop is clearer.

`collect` is the terminal operation that turns a stream back into something concrete: a list, a map, a string, a summary. It takes a **Collector**, a recipe for mutable reduction: create a container, add elements to it, merge containers (for parallel runs), and optionally transform the container into the final result. The `Collectors` utility class provides about forty ready-made recipes. Knowing five of them well covers most of what a backend developer writes: `toList`/`toSet`, `toMap`, `groupingBy`, `partitioningBy` and `joining`.

The examples use a small bookshop.

blocks.text:
### groupingBy: the workhorse

`groupingBy(classifier)` builds a `Map<K, List<T>>`: the classifier function computes the key for each element, equal keys share a bucket. The real power is the second argument, a **downstream collector** applied to each bucket. The elements of a group are not just collected into a list; they flow into whatever collector you give:

- `counting()` gives `Map<K, Long>` (group sizes).
- `summingInt(f)`, `averagingInt(f)`, `summarizingDouble(f)` give per-group statistics.
- `mapping(f, downstream)` transforms elements before collecting them (titles instead of books).
- `filtering(p, downstream)` and `flatMapping(f, downstream)` (Java 9) filter or flatten inside the group. Note the difference from a `filter` before the grouping: `filtering` keeps a group with a count of 0, a pre-`filter` drops the group entirely. In the output above, `HISTORY=1` stays even though only one book matched; with a pre-filter on a category that had no match the key would be missing.
- `maxBy(comparator)` / `minBy` give `Optional<T>` per group.
- Another `groupingBy` gives multi-level grouping, `Map<K1, Map<K2, V>>`.

The three-argument form `groupingBy(classifier, mapFactory, downstream)` lets you choose the map type. The default is a `HashMap`, with no ordering guarantee; the listing used `TreeMap::new` to keep the output stable. An `EnumMap` factory (`() -> new EnumMap<>(Category.class)`) is the right choice for an enum key.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: If you pass `collect(groupingBy(f, TreeMap::new, ...))` directly as the argument of `System.out.println(...)`, the compiler reports "inference variable R has incompatible bounds", because `println` is overloaded and inference gets confused. That is why `Col1` prints through a tiny `show(Object)` helper. In your own code, assign the result to a typed variable first.

### partitioningBy

`partitioningBy(predicate)` is a `groupingBy` with a boolean classifier, with two differences: the map always contains both keys `false` and `true` (even when a side is empty, with an empty list or count 0), and it accepts a downstream collector in the same way. Use it when you want "the ones that match and the ones that do not".

### joining, summarizing, collectingAndThen

`joining(delimiter, prefix, suffix)` concatenates `CharSequence` elements using a `StringBuilder`, so map to strings first. `summarizingInt/Long/Double` return a statistics object with count, sum, min, max and average in one pass. `collectingAndThen(downstream, finisher)` applies a function to the final result: the classic use is wrapping a list in an unmodifiable view. Since Java 10 there are also `toUnmodifiableList/Set/Map` and, since 16, `Stream.toList()`.

### toMap and its pitfalls

`toMap(keyFn, valueFn)` is convenient and has three well-known traps, two of which the listing triggers:

1. **Duplicate keys** throw `IllegalStateException: Duplicate key Austen (attempted merging values Emma and` `Persuasion)`. If duplicates are possible, provide a *merge function* as the third argument: `(a, b) -> a + "|" + b`, or `(a, b) -> a` to keep the first.
2. **Null values** throw `NullPointerException` (the implementation uses `HashMap.merge`). Wrap with `Optional` or filter them out first. (`Col2` below demonstrates this.)
3. **The result map is a** `HashMap` with unspecified order. Use the four-argument form with `TreeMap::new` or `LinkedHashMap::new` when order matters.

If you also need to group and the values are lists, prefer `groupingBy`, which handles duplicate keys by design.

### teeing: two collectors, one pass

`Collectors.teeing(c1, c2, merger)` (Java 12) feeds every element to two collectors and combines their results. It removes the need to traverse a stream twice, which is impossible anyway since a stream is one-shot. The listing used it to get the shortest and longest book in one pass; common uses are "count and sum", "min and max", or `(sum, count)` to compute an average by hand.

### Writing your own Collector

A `Collector<T, A, R>` has four functions: **supplier** (create the mutable container `A`), **accumulator** (add one element `T`), **combiner** (merge two containers, used by parallel streams) and **finisher** (convert `A` to the result `R`). `Collector.of(...)` builds one from lambdas. If the container is already the result, use the overload without a finisher; it marks the collector `IDENTITY_FINISH`.

#### What to notice

- `topN` keeps a bounded min-heap: every time the heap grows past `n`, the smallest element is removed. The combiner merges two heaps and trims, which is why the parallel run over 1000 numbers returns the same `[1000, 999, 998]`.
- A correct combiner is not optional. If it were wrong (say, it returned the first container), the sequential run would still look fine and only the parallel one would give wrong answers. Test collectors with `.parallel()`.
- `groupingBy` rejects a `null` key with `element cannot be mapped to a null key`.
- The empty characteristics set `[]` means: not concurrent, not unordered, and the finisher is needed.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Before writing a custom collector, check whether `teeing`, `mapping`, `reducing`, `collectingAndThen` or a chain of existing ones already does the job. Custom collectors are mainly for a library or for a hot path where a purpose-built accumulator matters. Java 24's gatherers (see the last chapter of this Part) cover the "intermediate operation" side that collectors cannot.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Reports and API responses are mostly `groupingBy` pipelines: "orders per customer", "revenue per day", "top 5 products per category". In a Spring service you typically convert entities to DTO records in a `map`, group, and return the `Map<String, List<Dto>>` as JSON. If the data lives in a database, do the aggregation in SQL: a stream pipeline over one million rows loaded into memory is a code smell.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you group a list of employees by department and get the average salary per department? `employees.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept,` `Collectors.averagingDouble(Employee::salary)))` gives `Map<Dept, Double>`. The first argument classifies, the second is a downstream collector applied per group. Pass `TreeMap::new` as the middle argument if you need sorted keys.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What can go wrong with `Collectors.toMap`? Duplicate keys throw `IllegalStateException` unless a merge function is given; a `null` value throws `NullPointerException`; the map type is an unspecified `HashMap` unless you pass a supplier.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A `Collector` is a four-part recipe (supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher) for mutable reduction.

- `groupingBy` with a downstream collector (`counting`, `summingInt`, `mapping`, `filtering`...) covers most aggregation; pass a map factory for ordering.
- `partitioningBy` always yields both `true` and `false`; `joining` builds strings; `teeing` computes two things in one pass.
- `toMap` fails on duplicate keys and null values unless you handle them; `toList()` on a stream gives an unmodifiable list.
- Custom collectors need a correct combiner; test them with `.parallel()`.

Adding `.parallel()` to a stream looks like free speed: one word, and the pipeline runs on all cores. Sometimes it is. Often it is slower, and occasionally it silently returns the wrong answer. This chapter explains what actually happens when a stream goes parallel, so that you can predict which of the three outcomes you will get instead of guessing.

### What .parallel() really does

A parallel stream changes only the *execution strategy* of the terminal operation. The pipeline you wrote stays the same. When the terminal operation starts, the runtime does three things.

1. **Split.** The source's `Spliterator` is asked to split itself with `trySplit()`, again and again, into smaller chunks, until the chunks are small enough or there are enough of them to keep all workers busy.
2. **Process.** Each chunk runs the whole pipeline (source to last intermediate operation, plus a partial terminal operation) as a task in a `ForkJoinPool`.
3. **Combine.** Partial results are merged pairwise on the way back up, using the *combiner* of the terminal operation: the combiner of a `Collector`, the second function of a three-argument `reduce`, and so on.

This is the same fork/join idea you will meet in the concurrency Part: divide, run independently, merge. A parallel stream is a fork/join computation whose "divide" step comes from the source and whose "merge" step comes from the terminal operation.

blocks.code:
$ java Par1.java
cores: 2
common pool parallelism: 1
threads used: [ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-#, main]
blocks.title: Which pool, how many workers?

blocks.text:
Output above is from the build machine, which has only 2 cores (typical output elsewhere will differ). By default, parallel streams use the JVM-wide **common pool**, `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`, whose parallelism defaults to the number of cores minus one. The calling thread helps too, which is why `main` appears in the list of threads: with one worker thread plus the caller, both cores are busy. Note what this implies: *every* parallel stream in the JVM, including those inside libraries and frameworks, shares this single pool.

You can change the common pool's size with `-Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=N` at startup. You cannot change it later.

### Ordering: what stays ordered and what does not

A common worry is that parallel means "random order". It does not, for most operations. A stream from a `List`, an array or `IntStream.range` is **ordered**, and the library preserves *encounter order* of the result for operations that are defined in terms of it: `collect` into a list, `toList()`, `findFirst`, `limit`, `skip`, `sorted`. What is *not* ordered is the **side** **effects**: the order in which `forEach` or `peek` lambdas happen to run.

blocks.title: Par1.java (excerpt)
Typical output (the forEach line changes from run to run)

blocks.text:
`forEachOrdered` forces the action to run in encounter order, but it gives away much of the benefit: elements may be computed in parallel, yet their actions are serialised and buffered. Use it when you must print or write in order; prefer collecting into a list and then iterating when you can.

Respecting order has a price. `limit(n)`, `skip(n)`, `findFirst` and `distinct` on an ordered parallel stream must coordinate chunks so that "the first n" really are the first n. If order does not matter to you, declare it with `unordered()`; the library can then use cheaper algorithms (for example `limit` may take *any* n elements, and `distinct` can use a concurrent set). `findAny` exists for the same reason: it may return any element, so it needs no coordination.

### The rules your lambdas must obey

Parallel streams make three promises, and each is conditional on your code. Break the condition and the promise is gone.

#### Rule 1: no shared mutable state

Lambdas passed to `map`, `filter`, `forEach` and friends run on several threads at once. If they write to a plain `ArrayList`, a `HashMap` or a counter, you have a data race (a topic of the concurrency Part).

blocks.title: Race.java

blocks.code:
$ java -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=3 Race.java
run 1: size = 632690
run 2: size = 705532
run 3: size = 569106
run 4: size = 387279
run 5: size = 592587
blocks.title: Typical output with three common-pool workers (numbers vary every run)

blocks.text:
One million elements were added; between 39 and 71 percent survived, and no exception was thrown. Two threads read the same `size`, both write to the same slot, and one of the adds is lost. Sometimes the same race instead throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` when the backing array is being grown. Worse, with a small input and few cores the race often does not show at all: on our two-core machine, 100 000 elements gave the correct size on every try. Code that "works on my laptop" is the typical way this bug reaches production.

The fix is not a synchronised list. It is to let the stream do the accumulating: `collect(Collectors.toList())` or `toList()`. Each worker fills its own private container and the combiner merges them, with no locks.

#### Rule 2: reduce functions must be associative, and the identity must be a true identity

`reduce(identity, op)` may be evaluated as `op(op(a, b), op(c, d))` instead of `op(op(op(a, b), c), d)`. That is only the same result when `op` is **associative**. The `identity` value is also used once per chunk, so it must satisfy `op(identity, x) == x`.

blocks.title: Par1.java (excerpt)

blocks.code:
$ java Par1.java
sequential: -5050
parallel  : 0
sequential: 20
parallel  : 50
blocks.title: Typical output (parallel results depend on how the source was split)

blocks.text:
Subtraction is not associative, so the parallel result is meaningless. The second pair is subtler: `10` is not an identity for addition (`0` is), so it is added once per chunk: sequentially once (giving 20), in parallel four times here (giving 50). A sequential run hides both mistakes. Rule of thumb: if you can write the same fold with `Collectors` or with `sum`, `max`, `count`, do that; hand-written `reduce` is where parallel bugs live.

#### Rule 3: behavioural parameters should be stateless and non-interfering

A lambda in a parallel pipeline must not depend on how many times it was called before, and must not modify the source while the stream runs. The first requirement is what makes `map(x -> counter++)` wrong; the second is what makes `list.stream().forEach(x -> list.add(x))` throw `ConcurrentModificationException` even sequentially. The previous chapter covered both; parallelism simply turns "wrong" into "wrong and random".

### When does parallel help?

Splitting, scheduling and merging cost something. A parallel stream wins only when the useful work outweighs that overhead. A simple rule of thumb is **N × Q**: the number of elements times the cost per element. If `N × Q` is large, parallelism pays. Five factors decide it.

rows: Many (thousands and up for heavy work, millions for light work)

$ java -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=3 Par2.java
CPU-heavy (count primes below 400000):
  sequential ms: 376
  parallel   ms: 357
Cheap work (sum 10 million ints):
  sequential ms: 15

Boxed sum, ArrayList vs LinkedList source (parallel):
  ArrayList  ms: 6
  LinkedList ms: 29
blocks.title: Typical output (measured on the build machine, 3 common-pool workers on 2 cores)

blocks.text:
Read these numbers carefully, because they teach three different things.

- **The prime count barely improved (376 to 357 ms).** The work is CPU-heavy, so it should scale, but two things hold it back here. First, the machine has two cores and was also running the harness. Second, the cost per number is wildly uneven (large primes take far longer than even numbers), so one chunk ends up with far more work than another and the others sit idle. Real speed-ups need free cores and evenly sized work; on an 8-core desktop the same code typically does much better.
- **The cheap sum improved even though it is trivial.** `IntStream.range(...).sum()` over primitives splits perfectly (a range is just two numbers) and has no boxing, so the overhead stays low. Do not generalise: 4 ms versus 15 ms is both tiny in absolute terms, and the sequential version here is already fast enough that nobody would care.
- **The source matters.** The same boxed sum over a `LinkedList` took about five times as long as over an `ArrayList`. An `ArrayList` splits in O(1) by index. A `LinkedList` has to walk to find the middle, so its spliterator splits by *copying* *batches* into arrays first.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Never trust a parallel speed-up (or slow-down) from a single `main` run Timings need warm-up, repetition and a quiet machine; the JIT compiler changes the cost of the same loop between its first and fifth run. For real decisions use JMH, the OpenJDK micro-benchmark harness, and measure in an environment shaped like production. And measure the right thing: a parallel stream that is 3x faster in isolation can make a loaded web server slower overall, since it steals cores from other requests.

### Pitfalls in production code

#### The shared common pool

The common pool has few threads and no per-caller isolation. If one request runs a parallel stream containing a blocking call (a database query, an HTTP request), it occupies common-pool workers for as long as that call takes, and every other parallel stream and `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync` without an explicit executor in the JVM queues behind it. This is one of the most common causes of "the whole service froze under load" stories involving parallel streams. Rule: **never block inside a parallel stream.** For I/O-bound fan-out use virtual threads or an executor you control (see the concurrency Part).

#### Using your own pool

There is no public `parallel(pool)` method. A widely-used trick is to start the terminal operation from inside a task running in your own `ForkJoinPool`; the stream's subtasks then run in that pool.

blocks.title: Par2.java (excerpt)

blocks.code:
$ java Par2.java
ForkJoinPool-1-worker-#
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The only thread names seen are `ForkJoinPool-1-worker-N`, not `commonPool`. Be aware that this behaviour is an implementation detail rather than a documented guarantee, so treat it as a pragmatic workaround and not a contract. It also does not solve the underlying issue that the work is CPU-bound and you still need to choose a sensible pool size.

#### Mixing parallel and sequential

A pipeline is either parallel or sequential as a whole. `parallel()` and `sequential()` just set a flag, and the **last call** **before the terminal operation wins**, whatever position it appears in. `stream.parallel().map(...).sequential().forEach(...)` runs sequentially from start to end.

#### Exceptions and debugging

An exception thrown in one worker propagates to the caller, but which one if several fail is not defined. Stack traces show `ForkJoinPool` frames and you lose the simple "one thread, one call stack" picture. Reproduce a problem sequentially first.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: When would you use a parallel stream, and when would you avoid it? Use it when the pipeline is CPU-bound, the data set is large, the source splits cheaply (array, `ArrayList`, range), the operations are stateless and associative, and there are spare cores. Avoid it for small data, I/O or blocking calls (they starve the shared common pool), `LinkedList` or `iterate` sources, order-sensitive operations, and anything that touches shared mutable state. Always measure; in a server also consider the effect on other requests.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In Spring Boot services you rarely see `parallelStream()` on request paths, because request threads should not fight over the common pool. Teams that need parallelism for heavy batch work typically use a dedicated executor, `CompletableFuture` with a named pool, or virtual threads for I/O fan-out, and keep streams sequential inside each task.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
`.parallel()` only changes how the terminal operation executes: split the source, run chunks in the common `ForkJoinPool`, merge with the combiner.

- Correctness first: no shared mutable state, associative reductions with a true identity, stateless lambdas.
- Order of results is preserved for ordered sources; the order of side effects is not. `forEachOrdered` and ordered `limit`/`findFirst` cost extra; `unordered()` and `findAny` relax this.
- Parallel helps for large, CPU-bound work on well-splitting sources (arrays, `ArrayList`, ranges) with free cores; it hurts for small or blocking work and `LinkedList`/`iterate` sources.
- The common pool is shared by the whole JVM: never block in it. Measure with JMH, not with one `main` run.

Intermediate operations such as `map`, `filter` and `limit` are a fixed menu. If you need "group every three elements", "running total" or "drop consecutive duplicates", the menu has nothing to offer, and you end up collecting to a list and looping, which defeats the pipeline. Collectors extend the *terminal* end of a stream; until recently there was no equivalent for the middle. **Stream Gatherers** (JEP 485) fill that gap: a `Gatherer` is a user-defined intermediate operation. They were previewed in Java 22 and 23 and became final in **Java 24**, so they are part of Java 25 LTS.

blocks.text: The build machine runs JDK 21, so none of the code in this chapter was executed. Listings are marked "(Java 24+; not run on 21)". They follow the Javadoc for `java.util.stream.Gatherer` and `Gatherers` (Java 25), and the sample results in comments are the ones given in that documentation. Run them yourself on JDK 24 or later before relying on them.

### Using the built-in gatherers

You attach a gatherer with the new `Stream.gather(Gatherer)` method. The class `java.util.stream.Gatherers` supplies five ready-made ones.

rows: Groups elements into lists of `n`; the last list may be shorter
Lists of `n` consecutive elements, each window dropping the oldest and adding the next
Like `reduce` but as an intermediate step: emits one element, the folded result, at the end
Prefix scan: emits every intermediate accumulated value
Maps with up to `max` concurrent virtual threads, keeping encounter order
blocks.caption: The built-in gatherers (Java 24+).

blocks.title: GatherDemo.java (Java 24+; not run on 21)

blocks.text:
What to notice: each result is still a stream, so gatherers compose with everything else (`filter(...).gather(...).map(...)`). `windowFixed` is the answer to the classic interview question "split a list into chunks of n" without index arithmetic. `windowSliding` gives you moving averages and "compare each element with the previous one" (adjacent pairs) checks. `scan` and `fold` differ in what they emit: `scan` one output per input, `fold` one output in total.

`mapConcurrent` deserves a note. It runs the mapper on virtual threads, at most `maxConcurrency` at a time, and still emits results in the original order. It is aimed at blocking work (calling a service per element) where a parallel stream would be the wrong tool, since it would block the shared common pool. It is a small, bounded fan-out that does not need `CompletableFuture`.

### How a gatherer works

A `Gatherer<T, A, R>` consumes elements of type `T`, may keep private state of type `A`, and pushes elements of type `R` downstream. It is built from up to four functions, which deliberately resemble a `Collector`:

rows: Creates the private state `A` for one run (for example a buffer or a counter). Omit it for stateless gatherers
Called for each element with `(state, element, downstream)`. May push zero, one or many results. Returns `true` to continue, `false` to say "no more input wanted" (short-circuit)
Merges two states, only needed so the gatherer can run in parallel. Omit it to make the gatherer sequential
Called once at the end with `(state, downstream)` to flush anything still buffered
blocks.caption: The four parts of a Gatherer.

blocks.text:
Two points make this more powerful than a plain `Collector` or `flatMap`. First, the integrator can push *several* elements or none, so it can express filtering, mapping, one-to-many and many-to-one in one place. Second, the integrator returns a boolean, so a gatherer can **short-circuit**, which a `Collector` never can. The factories are `Gatherer.ofSequential(...)` (no combiner, always run sequentially) and `Gatherer.of(...)` (with a combiner, may run in parallel); each has overloads that omit the initializer, the finisher or both.

### Writing a custom gatherer

A typical need that `Stream` lacks: remove *consecutive* duplicates (`1 1 2 2 2 1` becomes `1 2 1`). `distinct()` is wrong because it removes the later 1 too. The gatherer needs one piece of state, the previous element.

blocks.title: Dedupe.java (Java 24+; not run on 21)

blocks.text:
What to notice: the state class `Last` is created freshly per stream run by the initializer, so the gatherer object itself is reusable and holds no mutable fields. `downstream.push(x)` sends one result on and returns `false` if the downstream does not want more (a later `limit`, for example), and returning that value from the integrator propagates the short-circuit. `Integrator.ofGreedy` marks an integrator that never stops the stream by itself, which lets the library skip checking the result. Use `Integrator.of` when your integrator can return `false`.

Gatherers also compose with `andThen`, and a gatherer that is stateless can be parallel. For anything else, remember the rule from the parallel chapter: if state depends on *encounter order* (like "previous element"), the gatherer must be sequential, and `ofSequential` states that honestly.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do Gatherers differ from Collectors? A `Collector` is a terminal operation: it consumes the whole stream and produces one final result. A `Gatherer` is an intermediate operation: it can emit many elements, keep state between elements, and short-circuit, and the pipeline continues after it. `windowFixed`, `scan` and custom stateful steps are the typical uses. They became final in Java 24 (JEP 485).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Gatherers (final in Java 24) are user-defined intermediate stream operations, attached with `Stream.gather`.

- Built-ins: `windowFixed`, `windowSliding`, `fold`, `scan`, `mapConcurrent` in `java.util.stream.Gatherers`.
- A custom gatherer has an optional initializer, an integrator that pushes zero or more outputs and may short-circuit, an optional combiner and an optional finisher.
- Use `ofSequential` when order-dependent state cannot be merged; `of` with a combiner permits parallel evaluation.
- Not runnable on JDK 21: test on 24 or later.

Lambdas and streams are tools, and tools can be used well or badly. This closing chapter of the Part is about judgement: when does a functional style make code simpler, when does it make it worse, and how do you handle the awkward cases (checked exceptions, state, errors) that the tutorials skip.

### Immutability and pure functions

A **pure function** returns a value that depends only on its arguments and has no side effects (no printing, no writing to fields, no I/O). Pure functions are easy to test (call and compare), easy to reuse, safe to run in parallel and safe to cache. Streams are designed around them: `map`, `filter`, `reduce` and `collect` assume their lambdas are pure, and the parallel chapter showed what happens when they are not.

Immutability supports this. Records, `List.of`, `Map.of`, `Stream.toList()` and `Collections.unmodifiableList` give you values that cannot change under you. A method that receives an immutable list and returns a new list cannot corrupt anything, and a lambda that captures only immutable values is trivially thread-safe. Practical rules:

- Transform instead of mutate: `names.stream().map(String::toUpperCase).toList()` rather than looping and calling `set`.
- Keep side effects at the edges: compute with streams, then print, save or send once, at the end, from ordinary code.
- A lambda that does more than a line or two should become a named method and be passed as a method reference. The name is documentation, and you can unit-test the method on its own.

### Composing behaviour

Functional interfaces carry default methods for composition. `Function.andThen` and `compose` chain functions, `Predicate.and`, `or` and `negate` combine conditions, `Comparator.thenComparing` chains sort keys. A function that returns a function is a way to "pre-fill" an argument (currying).

blocks.title: Fx.java (excerpt)

blocks.code:
$ java Fx.java
28
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Read `pipeline` from the inside out: `compose(x -> x - 1)` runs first (10 becomes 9), then `add5` (14), then `andThen(x ->` `x * 2)` (28). Mixing `compose` and `andThen` in one expression is correct but easy to misread; in your own code prefer one direction.

### The checked exception problem

`java.util.function` interfaces declare no checked exceptions. The following does not compile, because `Files.readString` throws `IOException`:

blocks.code:
// does not compile: unreported exception java.io.IOException
paths.stream().map(p -> Files.readString(p)).toList();
blocks.title: Broken.java

blocks.text:
There is no perfect answer, only trade-offs. These are the options, in the order you should reach for them.

1. **Handle it inside the lambda.** If you can recover (use a default, log and skip), write a `try/catch` in a small named helper method that returns `Optional` or a default, and use a method reference to it.
2. **Wrap in an unchecked exception.** Convert to `UncheckedIOException` or your own runtime exception and let the whole pipeline abort. This is the right choice when the failure means the operation cannot continue.
3. **Return a result type.** Make each step return a value that represents success or failure and decide later. This keeps the pipeline going and lets you report all failures.

The listing below shows options 2 and 3 together.

blocks.title: Fx.java

blocks.code:
$ java Fx.java
5
6
stopped: java.io.FileNotFoundException: missing.txt
ok 5
ok 6
failed: missing.txt
ok 5
total of successes = 16
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text: What to notice: with the wrapper, elements before the failure were processed (`5`, `6`), the failure aborted the stream, and the original checked exception is preserved as the cause. With `Result`, all four names were processed, the failure is just a value, and the sealed interface plus pattern `switch` makes the compiler check that you handled both cases. The result-type approach is how most functional codebases do error handling in pipelines. (The record-pattern `switch` is in its own method because a `javac` 21 code-generation bug crashed the compiler when the same `switch` sat inside a lambda; this is fixed in later versions, so you usually need not worry.)

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Do not hide checked exceptions with "sneaky throw" tricks Generic tricks that throw a checked exception without declaring it compile, but callers cannot catch it by type in a way the compiler understands, and tools and colleagues will be surprised. Wrap in an unchecked exception with the original as `cause`.

### Streams versus loops

A stream is not automatically better than a loop. Choose by readability, and by what has to happen to the data.

rows: Data flows through filter, map, group, aggregate steps
You need several results from one pass with shared state
The steps read as a sentence
You need `break`, `continue`, labelled jumps or early `return` in the middle
Collectors express the result (group, partition, join)
You modify local variables (streams require effectively final)
The data is large and pure parallelism may help
You throw or handle checked exceptions per element
blocks.caption: Choosing between a stream pipeline and a loop.

blocks.text: An honest test: if the pipeline has more than about five stages, or any lambda is multi-line, extract methods or reconsider. Compare these two ways to find the first long name in uppercase:

blocks.title: Style.java

blocks.code:
$ java Style.java
Optional[CHARLOTTE]
Optional[CHARLOTTE]
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
Both are fine here; the stream version states *what* without index or flag. The advantage grows with the number of stages. Other common mistakes:

- **Side effects in** `map` **or** `peek` to "do work" (for example `map(x -> { list.add(x); return x; })`). Streams may skip, reorder or repeat such calls (the streams chapter warned that `count()` may skip `map` entirely when it can compute the size directly from the source).
- `stream().forEach(list::add)` instead of `collect` or `toList()`: harmless sequentially, a bug in parallel.
- **Streaming a tiny collection in a hot path.** A stream pipeline allocates several objects. Irrelevant in business code, relevant in a tight inner loop; profile before optimising.
- **Overusing** `Optional.get()`**, and** `Optional` **fields**: see the Optional chapter.
- **Boxing in numeric pipelines.** Prefer `mapToInt`, `IntStream` and `sum()` over `Stream<Integer>` with `reduce(0,` `Integer::sum)`.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In a Spring Boot codebase you will see streams in service-layer mapping code (`entities.stream().map(this::toDto).toList()`), in building maps for lookups (`Collectors.toMap`, `groupingBy`), and in tests. You will see plain loops in performance-sensitive and I/O-heavy code, and `Optional` returned by repository methods such as `findById`. Method references to small mapping methods are the idiom that keeps these readable.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Prefer pure functions and immutable data in pipelines; keep side effects at the edges.

- Extract non-trivial lambdas into named methods and use method references.
- Checked exceptions: catch in a helper, wrap in an unchecked exception, or return a `Result`-like value.
- Streams are best for filter/map/group/aggregate flows; loops win when you need early exits, several results or local mutation.
- Avoid side effects in `map`/`peek`, and avoid `forEach(list::add)`; use `collect`/`toList()`.
#### Lambdas and Functional Interfaces

items.question: What is the type of the expression `x -> x + 1`?
items.answer: It has no standalone type; it takes the type of its target, which must be a functional interface (for example `Function<Integer,Integer>` or `UnaryOperator<Integer>`).

items.question: What does this print? `Function<Integer,Integer> f = x -> x + 1; Function<Integer,Integer> g = x -> x *` `2; System.out.println(f.compose(g).apply(3));`
items.answer: `7`. `compose` runs `g` first (3 times 2 = 6) and then `f` (6+1 = 7).

items.question: Why does this not compile, and what is a good fix? `int n = 0; list.forEach(s -> n++);`
items.answer: `n` is modified so it is not effectively final. Fix: avoid mutation, e.g. `int n = list.size()` or `list.stream().mapToInt(String::length).sum()`; for threads use `AtomicInteger`.

items.question: Name the four kinds of method reference and give a one-line example of each.
items.answer: Static `Integer::parseInt`; bound `System.out::println`; unbound `String::length`; constructor `ArrayList::new` (also `int[]::new`).

items.question: In a class `Box` with a field `int size`, does `this.size` inside a lambda in one of its methods refer to the lambda or to the `Box`? What about inside an anonymous class?
items.answer: In a lambda `this` is the enclosing `Box`, so `this.size` works. In an anonymous class `this` is the anonymous object, and you must write `Box.this.size`.

items.question: How many extra `.class` files does the compiler produce for a class containing three lambdas, and where does the lambda code go?
items.answer: None. The bodies become private synthetic methods (`lambda$main$0` and so on) inside the same class; the interface implementations are hidden classes generated at run time via `invokedynamic`.

blocks.text: #### Optional: Modelling "No Result"

items.question: What does `Optional.ofNullable(null).map(String::length).orElse(0)` return?
items.answer: `0`. The empty `Optional` stays empty through `map`, and `orElse` supplies 0.

items.question: What is wrong with `public void setName(Optional<String> name)` as a setter?
items.answer: A parameter of type `Optional` can itself be `null`, forces wrapping on every caller and adds nothing over a nullable parameter or an overload. `Optional` is for return types.

items.question: In `opt.orElse(load())`, when does `load()` run? How do you change that?
items.answer: Always, before `orElse` is called, even when the value is present. Use `orElseGet(this::load)` to make it lazy.

items.question: Given `Optional<String> o = Optional.of("a");` what does `o.map(s -> (String) null).isPresent()` print?
items.answer: `false`. When the mapping function returns `null`, `map` returns `Optional.empty()`.

items.question: You have `List<Integer> ids` and `Optional<Member> find(int id)`. Write one stream expression producing the list of members that exist.
items.answer: `ids.stream().map(this::find).flatMap(Optional::stream).toList()`.

items.question: Why should you not call `get()` without `isPresent()`, and what should you use?
items.answer: `get()` throws `NoSuchElementException` when empty and hides that risk. Use `orElseThrow()` (or `orElseThrow(Supplier)`), `orElse`, `orElseGet`, or `ifPresent`.

blocks.text: #### Streams: Fundamentals

items.question: What does this print? `Stream.of(1, 2, 3).peek(x -> System.out.print(x)).map(x -> x * 2);`
items.answer: Nothing. There is no terminal operation, so no element is ever processed.

items.question: What does this print? `Stream.of(5, 6, 7, 1, 8).takeWhile(x -> x > 4).toList()` and what would `filter(x ->` `x > 4)` give instead?
items.answer: `[5, 6, 7]`; `filter` would give `[5, 6, 7, 8]` because it keeps testing after the first failure.

items.question: A colleague writes `Stream<String> s = list.stream(); s.forEach(...); s.forEach(...);`. What happens?
items.answer: The second `forEach` throws `IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed`.

items.question: Why is `Stream.iterate(1, x -> x + 1).sorted().limit(3).toList()` a bug?
items.answer: `sorted()` is a barrier needing all elements, and the source is infinite, so it never finishes (it eventually runs out of memory).

items.question: Choose `map` or `flatMap`: turning `List<Order>` into all `OrderLine`s when `Order.lines()` returns a `List<OrderLine>`.
items.answer: `flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream())`, because each order maps to many lines.

items.question: Why is `IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).sum()` preferable to `Stream.of(1,2,3,4,5).reduce(0, Integer::sum)`?
items.answer: It uses primitive `int` all the way (no boxing), states the intent directly and is shorter.

blocks.text: #### Collectors

items.question: What does `Stream.of("a", "bb", "cc").collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length,` `Collectors.counting()))` return?
items.answer: A `Map<Integer, Long>` equal to `{1=1, 2=2}`.

items.question: What is the difference between `groupingBy(f)` and `partitioningBy(p)` regarding keys in the result when no element satisfies `p`?
items.answer: `partitioningBy` always has both `true` and `false` keys (the empty side maps to an empty list / zero); `groupingBy` only has keys for which at least one element exists.

items.question: What goes wrong here, and how do you fix it? `Stream.of("x", "x").collect(Collectors.toMap(s -> s, s ->` `1))`
items.answer: `IllegalStateException: Duplicate key x`. Pass a merge function: `Collectors.toMap(s -> s, s -> 1,` `Integer::sum)`.

items.question: Name the four functions of a `Collector`. Which one only matters for parallel streams?
items.answer: Supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher. The combiner is used to merge partial results of parallel streams.

items.question: What does `r` hold? `String r = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4).collect(Collectors.teeing(Collectors.counting(),` `Collectors.summingInt(i -> i), (n, s) -> s + "/" + n));`
Why is `groupingBy(Employee::dept)` a bad choice if `dept` may be `null`?
items.answer: A `null` classifier result throws `NullPointerException: element cannot be mapped to a null key`. Map nulls to a sentinel such as `"UNKNOWN"` first.

blocks.text: #### Parallel Streams and Performance

items.question: What does the following print the first time you run it, and is the output guaranteed? `IntStream.rangeClosed(1,` `5).parallel().forEach(System.out::print);`
items.answer: It prints the digits 1 to 5 in some order (e.g. `31245` or `12345`); the order of side effects in `forEach` is not guaranteed on a parallel stream. Use `forEachOrdered` for encounter order.

items.question: Why does `Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4).parallel().reduce(10, Integer::sum)` not return 20 in general?
items.answer: The identity `10` is applied once per chunk, not once overall, and the number of chunks depends on the split. Sequentially you get 20; in parallel you can get 50 or other values. The identity must be `0` for addition.

items.question: A colleague "fixes" a data race in a parallel `forEach` by switching the target to `Collections.synchronizedList`. Why is this still a poor design?
items.answer: The result is now correct but contended: all workers queue on one lock, so you lose most of the parallel speed-up, and the element order is nondeterministic. Collecting with `toList()` or a `Collector` uses per-worker containers and a combiner.

items.question: Which is better for parallel processing, an `ArrayList` of 5 million elements or a `LinkedList` of the same, and why?
items.answer: The `ArrayList`: it splits by index in constant time and has good cache locality. A `LinkedList` must traverse to split.

items.question: What does this pipeline do: `list.stream().parallel().map(f).sequential().forEach(g)`?
items.answer: The whole pipeline runs sequentially, because the last of `parallel()`/`sequential()` before the terminal operation decides the mode for the entire pipeline.

items.question: Why is a blocking database call inside `parallelStream().forEach(...)` dangerous?
items.answer: Blocked workers occupy the shared common pool, so other parallel streams and async tasks in the whole JVM stall behind them.

blocks.text: #### Stream Gatherers

items.question: What is the difference between `Gatherers.scan` and `Gatherers.fold`?
items.answer: `scan` emits every intermediate accumulation (one output per input); `fold` emits only the final accumulated value (exactly one element).

items.question: What would `Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).gather(Gatherers.windowFixed(2)).toList()` return?
items.answer: `[[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]`: the last window is smaller.

items.question: Why can a `Gatherer` short-circuit while a `Collector` cannot?
items.answer: The integrator returns a boolean, and `false` signals "stop sending me input", while a `Collector`'s accumulator returns nothing and the pipeline always feeds it every element.

items.question: In which Java release did gatherers become a final feature, and which method attaches one to a stream?
items.answer: Java 24 (JEP 485); `Stream.gather(Gatherer)`.

items.question: When must you create a gatherer with `ofSequential` and not `of`?
items.answer: When the logic depends on encounter order or on state that cannot be merged by a combiner, as with "previous element" state.

blocks.text: #### Functional Style in Practice

items.question: What does `Function<Integer,Integer> f = x -> x + 1; f.compose((Integer x) -> x * 2).andThen(x -> x` `* 10).apply(3)` return?
items.answer: `compose` runs first: 3 \* 2 = 6, then `f`: 7, then `andThen`: 70. The result is 70.

items.question: Why does `names.stream().map(n -> Files.readString(Path.of(n)))` not compile, and what are two ways to fix it?
items.answer: `readString` throws the checked `IOException` and `Function.apply` declares none. Fix by catching inside a helper method, wrapping in `UncheckedIOException`, or returning a result type.

items.question: What is wrong here, and what is the idiomatic fix? `List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();` `names.stream().filter(n -> n.length() > 3).forEach(out::add);`
items.answer: It mutates an external list from inside the pipeline, which is a data race if the stream becomes parallel. Use `.collect(Collectors.toList())` or `.toList()`.

items.question: Name two situations where a plain loop is the better choice than a stream.
items.answer: Examples: you need `break`/early exit mixed with several local mutable variables, or per-element checked exception handling, or the logic is simply clearer as a loop.

items.question: Why is a pure function easier to run in a parallel stream?
items.answer: It has no shared state or side effects, so chunks cannot interfere with each other and the order in which they run does not change the result.
